clarity-of-mind-omah-lay-s-introspective:
Four years after Boy Alone reshaped the emotional lane of Afrobeats, Stanley Omah Didia, popularly known as Omah Lay, returns with his long-awaited sophomore album titled Clarity of Mind.

Clarity of Mind feels like the songs of a man who knows his flaws and is introspective enough to understand how dangerous or reckless they are, yet addicted enough to return to them. That tension between awareness and indulgence runs through the project and shapes much of the emotion that defines the album.

It is a follow-up to the critically acclaimed Boy Alone that dropped four years ago, which did incredibly well both as a collector’s classic and as a herald of a shift in Afrobeats culture — with both the numbers and its impact. By the night Clarity of Mind dropped, the project had already clocked in at over 3.6 billion streams across major platforms:

• 1.31 billion streams on Spotify

• 915 million plays on YouTube Music

• 690 million streams on Audiomack

• 681 million streams on Boomplay

Would he top these figures with his new project? I don’t own a crystal ball to see that far into the future. Hence, this review will focus on the merits of what it knows and has heard on the new tape.

Omah Lay is a gifted artist — that much is not in doubt. He has a way of weaving melodies in a manner that is peculiar to him, matched with deep lyrics that require introspection, and Clarity of Mind delivers on that whilst breaking the mould of whatever you may have thought he and his sound were.

On this project, Omah Lay didn’t necessarily reinvent the wheel of his sound — he simply switched gears.

Clarity of Mind runs for approximately 33 minutes and opens with Artificial Happiness, a melodious groove that sets the tempo for what to expect from the album.

Artificial Happiness, produced by Tempo, opens with his conversation with marijuana/Igbo. He croons, ‘Before morning, the feeling will wash off / But tonight, we will die at the warfront,’ his lyrics capturing a scene fuelled by weed, all whilst the ‘Blood of Jesus’ echoes through the ad-libs.

Omah Lay threads different topics in melody and melancholy, and that emotional numbness becomes clearer on Don’t Love Me, where he sings lines like ‘Hennessy no dey hit me again / Igbo no dey high me again.’ Here he also talks about his relationship with women and the lengths he goes to get in their panties, including renting a five-bedroom rooftop apartment for two years for one.

Still on the theme of women, Omah Lay sings on Waist: ‘I’m making wrong decisions/Anytime I see ikebe,’ going further to say that it was also what killed the biblical Samson — perhaps an admittance of his flaws and an acceptance of his fate.

The only feature on the album comes on track six, where a budding artist called Elmah appears on Coping Mechanism. Elmah’s voice and lyrics offer softness to the record before Stanley delivers a verse that feels different from the others on the album — vulnerable and emotionally charged. Lines like ‘Unhappiness is hurting me / I can’t feel my shoulders anymore / Is it ‘cause I carry all the load?’ stand out.

He admits that he tours the world looking for where he belongs. It’s relatable and requires some quietude to properly soak in.

The next two songs pull you away from those introspective thoughts as Stanley delivers two upbeat, danceable records in Julia and Waist, the latter of which was a lead single for the album.

Four more songs — Mary Go Round, I AM, Holy Ghost, and Amen — complete the album. The project was largely produced by Tempo, who worked on seven tracks.

Taken together, Clarity of Mind presents the music of a man who recognises his excesses and contradictions but continues to wrestle with them in real time. Lines like ‘Everybody know say smoking is dangerous / But once I see marijua’, I go light am / Money is the root of evil but every day I pack am’ capture that inner conflict perfectly.

Overall, it’s a strong album with impressive replay value. More importantly, Clarity of Mind confirms what many already suspected — Omah Lay remains one of the most emotionally distinct voices in modern Afrobeats.

Rating: 8/10

Favourite songs:

• Artificial Happiness

• I AM

• Canada Breeze

• Don’t Love Me

• Water Spirit

Notable mentions:

• Coping Mechanism

• Jah Jah Knows

• Julia
odeluwa:
The world now knows about a great writer, standing tall and strong, but not everyone knows she’s a phoenix that rose from the ashes. This is the story of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie.

When Chimamanda was a little girl growing up on a university campus in Nsukka, eastern Nigeria, she wrote stories. All the characters in them had blue eyes, played in the snow, and ate apples. She had never seen snow. She had never eaten an apple. But every book she could find was filled with people who did, and so she wrote what she had been taught, without knowing she had been taught it.

That quiet early distortion, the way the world tried to tell her that her own life was not the stuff of literature, would later become the seed of one of the most important and widely watched TED talks in history. But first, it would take years of rejection, doubt, displacement, and stubbornness to get there.

A Girl Who Wrote About Snow She Had Never Seen

Think of a house in Nsukka with five other children in it. The noise of it. The constant, joyful chaos of a family where someone is always eating, always arguing, always laughing too loudly at the dinner table. Chimamanda grew up in that house, the fifth of six, in a university town in eastern Nigeria where her father taught and her mother administered, and books were simply part of the furniture. She was reading by four. Writing not long after. But here is the thing nobody tells you about a child who grows up surrounded by books: the books she found were almost all written by people who did not look like her, did not live where she lived, had never heard the sound of her language. And so, without knowing she was doing it, she learnt to disappear herself from her own imagination. The characters she wrote had blue eyes. They played in the snow. They ate apples for lunch. She had never seen snow. She had never eaten an apple. She wrote them anyway, because that was what stories were, apparently. Stories happened to other people, in other places. Not here. Not her.

There was also the war. The Nigerian Civil War ended seven years before she was born, but it lived in her family the way wars always do — not as history but as a hush, as names not spoken at the table, as grandfathers she never met. That particular silence would take her years to understand and a whole novel to write through. But that came later. First, there was the small matter of deciding what kind of person she was going to be.

She tried medicine first. Enrolled at the University of Nigeria in Nsukka, sat through lectures, and committed to the path that looked responsible. A year and a half in, she stopped. Not because she failed. Because she knew, with the clarity that only comes once, that she was in the wrong room. She was nineteen when she packed for America. Philadelphia. Drexel University. She stepped off a plane into a winter that had nothing in common with anything she had ever felt on her skin, and into a country that had no idea what to do with her. She was not African-American. She was not the Africa of charity posters or adventure films. She was a girl from Nsukka who wanted to write novels, and the city went about its business without noticing her at all. That invisibility, she would come to understand, was its own kind of education.

The Manuscript They Said Was Too African

She was writing a novel. Purple Hibiscus, a story about a teenage girl, a devout and violent father, and a family holding its breath in post-military Nigeria. She wrote it in America, in the specific loneliness of being far from home and unsure whether home would ever make it onto the page. When she sent it out, the responses she got back were not always rejections exactly. Some of them were worse than rejections. They were suggestions. Move the story to America. Change the setting. Make it somewhere readers can picture. Your people, your streets, your language — these are obstacles. Sand them down. Make yourself easier to digest.

She did not do any of those things. She kept the setting. She kept the language. She kept the red dust and the generator hum and the particular way grief moves through an Igbo family. She kept all of it, because the whole point, she understood this even then, even at twenty-something in a cold American city, was that there was nothing wrong with it. There was nothing that needed to be removed, relocated, or made more palatable. The story was exactly where it was supposed to be.

‘All fiction is political simply because the writing does not exist in a vacuum.’

She kept submitting. Eventually, a small independent publisher called Algonquin Books said yes. When Purple Hibiscus came out in 2003, the people who read it understood immediately that something different had arrived.

What She Made of It

What came next is the part people know, or think they know. The prizes. The fellowships. The TED talk that has been watched by tens of millions of people and translated into more languages than she probably expected when she stood on that stage and began talking about the stories we tell ourselves about other people. Half of a Yellow Sun, the novel she wrote about the war that swallowed her grandfathers, won prizes too. But the thing about listing prizes is that it reduces what she actually did to a set of credentials, and credentials are not the point.

The point is what she changed. Before her, a novel set in Nigeria was often received in the West as a document — evidence of a place, proof of a struggle, useful for understanding Africa. After her, it became possible for more people to simply read African fiction as fiction. As a story. As the thing you pick up because you want to spend time inside another person’s life, not because you are trying to learn something about a foreign country. That shift is hard to measure and easy to underestimate. It is also, quietly, enormous.

She turned down a national honour from the Nigerian government in 2022. No press conference. No lengthy explanation. Just: no. That too is consistent. She has never wanted the version of success that requires you to become agreeable.

I keep thinking about the girl in Nsukka. The one writing characters with blue eyes. She was not failing at her imagination; she was doing exactly what she had been taught. The miracle is not that she eventually stopped. The miracle is that she noticed she had started. That she looked at the page, and then looked at herself, and understood that the distance between the two was not inevitable. It was a choice someone else had made for her. And she could unmake it.

That is what she did. She unmade it. And then she wrote something true instead.

The world will tell you who you were supposed to be, but it’s up to you to choose something greater.
